/-!
# Packing

This file contains a number of open problems related to the minimal size of a square (or circle)
that can contain a given number of unit squares (or circles).
In each case, we provide a known upper bound, and ask for the least such size.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia on packing of squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing)
- [Wikipedia on packing of circles in a circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_packing_in_a_circle)
- [Wikipedia on packing of circles in a square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_packing_in_a_square)
- Friedman, Erich (2009), "Packing unit squares in squares: a survey and new results",
  Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 1000, Dynamic Survey 7
- Pirl, U. (1969),
  ["Der Mindestabstand von $n$ in der Einheitskreisscheibe gelegenen Punkten"](https://doi.org/10.1002/mana.19690400110),
  Mathematische Nachrichten, 40: 111–124
- A website with visualizations of packings:
  [link](https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/)
-/

@[expose] public section

open EuclideanGeometry

open scoped NNReal

universe u

namespace SquarePacking

/--
A square of a particular side length as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
Not including border, so that squares that touch at the border are disjoint,
but a square internal to another shape is a subset of that shape.
-/
def Square (side : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  {p : ℝ² | 0 < p 0 ∧ p 0 < side ∧ 0 < p 1 ∧ p 1 < side}

/--
The unit square as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
-/
def UnitSquare : Set ℝ² := Square 1

/--
A circle of a particular radius as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
The radius is a nonnegative real, so that `Circle r` is always the disc of radius $r$.
Not including border, so that circles that touch at the border are disjoint,
but a circle internal to another shape is a subset of that shape.
-/
def Circle (r : ℝ≥0) : Set ℝ² :=
  {p : ℝ² | p 0 ^ 2 + p 1 ^ 2 < (r : ℝ) ^ 2}

/--
The unit circle as a subset of the Euclidean plane.
-/
def UnitCircle : Set ℝ² := Circle 1

/--
A structure representing a packing of `n` isometric embeddings
of a set `s` inside a (presumably larger) set `S`.
-/
structure Packing (n : ℕ) (s : Set ℝ²) (S : Set ℝ²) where
  /-- The isometric equivalences
  that represent the transformations of the base shape to their locations in the packing. -/
  embeddings : Fin n → (ℝ² ≃ᵢ ℝ²)
  /-- The images of the embeddings are pairwise disjoint -/
  disjoint : Pairwise fun i j => Disjoint (embeddings i '' s) (embeddings j '' s)
  /-- The images of the embeddings are all inside the larger set `S` -/
  inside : ∀ i : Fin n, embeddings i '' s ⊆ S

/--
The degenerate circle is empty.
-/
@[category test, AMS 51]
theorem circle_zero : Circle 0 = ∅ := by
  ext p
  simp only [Circle, Set.mem_ofPred_eq, Set.mem_empty_iff_false, iff_false, not_lt,
    NNReal.coe_zero, zero_pow, ne_eq, OfNat.ofNat_ne_zero, not_false_eq_true]
  positivity

/--
Eleven unit squares can be packed into a square of side length < 3.877084.

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem eleven_square_packing_in_square_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 11 UnitSquare (Square 3.877084)) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest square that can contain 11 unit squares?

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_eleven_square_packing_in_square :
    IsLeast {x : ℝ | Nonempty (Packing 11 UnitSquare (Square x))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Seventeen unit squares can be packed into a square of side length < 4.6756.

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem seventeen_square_packing_in_square_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square 4.6756)) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest square that can contain 17 unit squares?

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_square)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_seventeen_square_packing_in_square :
    IsLeast {x : ℝ | Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square x))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Three unit squares can be packed into a circle of radius $(5 \sqrt{17}) / 16 \approx 1.288$.

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_circle)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem three_square_packing_in_circle_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 3 UnitSquare (Circle ((5 * NNReal.sqrt 17) / 16))) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest circle that can contain 3 unit squares?

Reference: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_packing#In_a_circle)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_three_square_packing_in_circle :
    IsLeast {r : ℝ≥0 | Nonempty (Packing 3 UnitSquare (Circle r))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Twenty-one unit circles can be packed into a square of side length < 9.359.

Reference: [Visualizations](https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/cirinsqu/)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem twenty_one_circle_packing_in_square_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 21 UnitCircle (Square 9.359)) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest square that can contain 21 unit circles?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_twenty_one_circle_packing_in_square :
    IsLeast {x : ℝ | Nonempty (Packing 21 UnitCircle (Square x))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
Fifteen unit circles can be packed into a circle of radius
$1 + \sqrt{6 + 2/\sqrt{5} + 4 \sqrt{1 + 2/\sqrt{5}}} \approx 4.521$.

Reference:
Graham RL, Lubachevsky BD, Nurmela KJ, Ostergard PRJ.
Dense packings of congruent circles in a circle. Discrete Math 1998;181:139–154.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 51]
theorem fifteen_circle_packing_in_circle_bound :
    Nonempty (Packing 15 UnitCircle
      (Circle (1 + NNReal.sqrt (6 + 2 / NNReal.sqrt 5 +
        4 * NNReal.sqrt (1 + 2 / NNReal.sqrt 5))))) := by
  sorry

/--
What is the smallest circle that can contain 15 unit circles?

Reference:
Graham RL, Lubachevsky BD, Nurmela KJ, Ostergard PRJ.
Dense packings of congruent circles in a circle. Discrete Math 1998;181:139–154.
[Pirl (1969)](https://doi.org/10.1002/mana.19690400110) conjectured this configuration to be optimal.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51]
theorem least_fifteen_circle_packing_in_circle :
    IsLeast {r : ℝ≥0 | Nonempty (Packing 15 UnitCircle (Circle r))} answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

end SquarePacking

findings.description: The docstring states a strict bound, “side length < 3.877084”, but the Lean statement gives a packing in `Square 3.877084`, hence only a non-strict upper bound. Using open interiors permits boundary contact; it does not imply that a smaller container works. The stated Lean bound itself is correct.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia, Square_packing#In_a_square, describes Trump's construction. The linked successor to Friedman's squares-in-squares page gives its side as 3.87708359002281…, strictly below 3.877084: https://kingbird.myphotos.cc/packing/squares_in_squares.html.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to “side length at most 3.877084”, or retain the strict wording and state `∃ x : ℝ, x < 3.877084 ∧ Nonempty (Packing 11 UnitSquare (Square x))`.

findings.description: The docstring says “side length < 4.6756”, whereas `Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square 4.6756))` states feasibility at 4.6756, not feasibility at a strictly smaller size. This is a documentation precision issue, not an incorrect numerical bound.
findings.source_evidence: Friedman's cited survey, Section 3, Figure 12, explicitly states `s(17) < 4.6756`: https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/DS7/html_1. The successor packing page gives 4.67553009360455….
findings.suggested_fix: Change “< 4.6756” to “at most 4.6756” in the docstring, or strengthen the statement to `∃ x : ℝ, x < 4.6756 ∧ Nonempty (Packing 17 UnitSquare (Square x))`.

findings.description: The docstring claims a square of side length strictly less than 9.359. The Lean declaration instead supplies a packing at side length 9.359, a non-strict upper bound. Boundary contact remains allowed despite the open-set definitions. The numerical upper bound is valid.
findings.source_evidence: The cited Friedman page lists `s = 9.358+` for 21 unit circles: https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/cirinsqu/. Its linked Packomania table gives the side-length ratio 9.3580199589…, below 9.359: https://www.packomania.com/csq/csq.html.
findings.suggested_fix: Use “side length at most 9.359” in the docstring, or state `∃ x : ℝ, x < 9.359 ∧ Nonempty (Packing 21 UnitCircle (Square x))`.

status_issues.source_status: Solved by K. J. Nurmela and P. R. J. Östergård in 1999. Their computer-aided optimality result includes 21 circles; the minimum square side for unit-radius circles is approximately 9.3580199589.
status_issues.evidence: The directly cited Friedman page says for n=21: “s = 9.358+; Proved by Nurmela and Östergård in 1999” (https://erich-friedman.github.io/packing/cirinsqu/). Their primary paper extends the solved range to n ≤ 27; Section 3 specifically explains the n=21 optimality proof, and Table 2 gives d21 ≈ 0.2718122553, corresponding to side length 2 + 2/d21 (https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/PL00009472.pdf).
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to `research solved` and cite Nurmela–Östergård (1999). Replace the answer placeholder with an exact specification of the established optimum when available; do not use the rounded bound 9.359 as the minimum.

reformulations.difference: The file represents squares and disks by their open interiors and requires disjoint images, rather than using closed bodies whose interiors do not overlap.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A closed unit square or disk is the closure of its interior, and each plane isometry is a homeomorphism. Taking closures converts containment of the placed interiors into containment of the closed bodies; taking interiors gives the converse. Homeomorphisms also preserve interiors, so disjointness is precisely the usual non-overlap condition, with boundary contact allowed. In /workspace/review/packing_equiv.lean I proved the general equivalence for regular-closed pieces and closed containers, and instantiated it for all four square/disk combinations used in the file.

sources_consulted: Graham, Lubachevsky, Nurmela and Östergård, Dense packings of congruent circles in a circle, Discrete Mathematics 181 (1998), 139–154; especially Sections 1–2, Figure 2 and Table 1. Full text: https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/98_01_circles.pdf. Bibliographic metadata also consulted through Crossref, Semantic Scholar and Elsevier.

Nurmela and Östergård, More Optimal Packings of Equal Circles in a Square, Discrete & Computational Geometry 22 (1999), 439–457; abstract, Sections 1 and 3, and Table 2. https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/PL00009472.pdf
review.notes: No substantive mathematical misformalization was found. All five numerical bounds and minimum-size formulations were checked. Lean experiments confirmed the Euclidean metric, Circle r = Metric.ball 0 r, nonemptiness of the unit shapes, exclusion of nonpositive square sizes and zero-radius containers for positive packings, distinctness of packed copies, and uniqueness of an IsLeast answer. Scratch checks and the packing-equivalence proofs compile successfully. Pirl's original full text was inaccessible; the relevant 15-circle statement was checked against the cited Wikipedia article and the accessible Graham et al. paper.
